To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
, in private value environments, the competitive mechanism is almost as efficient as the first-price auction and, in common value environments, the second-price auction is almost as efficient.
, under private information, the competitive mechanism is approximately efficient in a large economy.

(1) the number of traders in the economy can be arbitrarily small and (2) the probability that a trader is non-strategic can be arbitrarily small, yet (3) a competitive mechanism can still lead to allocations that are close (in the sense of the approximation) to those of the true economy with high probability.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how much information is needed to achieve efficiency in a large economy.
the efficiency of competitive mechanisms when there is private information about traders’ preferences.
the efficiency of competitive mechanisms when the number of traders becomes large.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in large economies with small probability of non-strategic traders, the competitive mechanism is a very good approximation of the competitive equilibrium.
, for a large enough number of traders, a competitive mechanism can achieve a good approximation of the efficient outcome of the true economy with high probability.
the competitive mechanism is approximately efficient.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, in the presence of private information, a small amount of strategic behavior is sufficient for the existence of a competitive mechanism that achieves a high degree of approximation to a competitive equilibrium.
, under private information, the efficiency properties of competitive markets are not affected by the size of the market.
the efficiency properties of competitive mechanisms are robust to the presence of strategic traders.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, even in a setting where traders have private information and are not required to be truthful, the efficiency properties of competitive mechanisms are preserved, and the number of traders required for this to happen does not need to grow with the size of the market.
, even in economies with private information, the efficiency properties of the competitive mechanism are preserved, provided that the economy is large enough.
the efficiency properties of competitive markets are robust to strategic behavior.
